cells.C: Purely from a Qualitative Data Analysis tool only, no ITDRPaaS applications
Purely as a qualitative data analysis method, the strongest general-purpose choice is Reflexive Thematic Analysis (RTA).
Why RTA is the best general tool

RTA systematically identifies and interprets recurring patterns of meaning across qualitative data, including interview transcripts, focus groups, written responses, field notes, and documents. It is especially effective when the research objective is to understand participants’ perceptions, interpretations, attitudes, or experiences without attempting to generate a formal theory (Braun & Clarke, 2006, 2021).
accommodates inductive, deductive, or combined coding;
recognizes the researcher’s active interpretive role;
provides a transparent six-phase analytical process;
works across many qualitative research designs;
produces themes that explain patterned meaning rather than merely summarizing topics.

cells.D: Read, reread, annotate, and become immersed in the data
Identify meaningful features throughout the dataset
Combine related codes into broader patterns of meaning
Test themes against coded excerpts and the complete dataset
Establish each theme’s central organizing concept, boundaries, and name
Integrate themes, evidence excerpts, interpretation, and scholarship

cells.C: RTA should not be reduced to counting repeated words or placing similar statements into topical folders. A theme must capture a pattern of shared meaning organized around a central concept (Braun & Clarke, 2021). Frequency can inform analysis, but the most frequent response is not automatically the most analytically significant.

cells.C: Use Reflexive Thematic Analysis when the analytical purpose is to interpret patterns of meaning across qualitative data. Use Generic Thematic Analysis only when a more descriptive, methodologically flexible analysis is required. If “tool” means software rather than analytical method, MAXQDA would be the strongest all-purpose qualitative analysis platform—but the software manages the evidence; it does not perform the scholarly interpretation.
